questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that resists its label
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a label can misrepresent the object it names
questions.stem: A transit planner's board in a northern depot pins an enamelled station-name tile under the heading Victorian signage, although the lettering matches a standard adopted only in the 1930s and the flange is thinner than earlier examples.

options.text: The label names the period the board wants the tile to illustrate, not the year the tile was made.
The tile is a Victorian original that was re-enamelled when the station was rebuilt in the 1930s.
options.misconception: assumes a re-enamelled tile keeps its original date

options.text: The label is a harmless matter of display taste, since the tile only needs to look right in the case.
options.misconception: believes a display label is a matter of taste

options.text: The board should drop the heading and date the tile by the date of the station it once named.
options.misconception: dates a building piece by the building's own history

questions.explanation: The tile follows a 1930s standard, so the label describes an era the board wants rather than the tile's making. Labels can be inherited or careless; the object's own features date it.
questions.hint: Ask which features of the object contradict the heading.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Dating by style
questions.learningObjective: Date a work by matching its features to a dated standard
questions.stem: The planning office compares two enamel platform signs: the first has rounded capitals and a single border line, the second uses squared capitals and a double border. The board knows the first design was standard from 1908 and the second from 1931, and asks which sign was made first and why.

options.text: The second sign, because squared capitals and a double border are a more advanced and so later design.
options.misconception: assumes a plainer look means a later date

options.text: The first sign, because its rounded capitals and single border follow the standard adopted in 1908.
Neither can be ordered, because each sign was made by a different contractor with its own habits.
options.misconception: assumes contractor habits erase design standards

options.text: The first sign, because older signs were always repainted rather than replaced once lettering changed.
options.misconception: believes repainting explains every design change

questions.explanation: A design standard with a known adoption date can date a sign whose features match it. Style helps because makers follow the fashions of their trade, not because later design is always more advanced.
questions.hint: Match the lettering to a standard with a known date.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Science that dates the support
questions.learningObjective: Explain what support analysis dates and what it leaves open
questions.stem: The planning office acquires a painted panel from a station refit. A dendrochronology report dates the oak to 1488, and the curator asks the board to explain why that figure dates the support rather than the picture painted on it.

answer.exemplar: Dendrochronology measures the growth rings of the timber itself, so the report dates the felling of the tree, and a panel could be stored, reused or held in stock for years afterwards. The picture on that wood is therefore likely later than the timber, and the two dates have to be recorded separately.

questions.explanation: Ring analysis dates the wood, and panels were often stored or reused before painting. The board should record the felling date and treat the painting as a later event.
questions.hint: A panel can outlive the tree it came from by decades.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the period in which two dated samples agree
questions.stem: A laboratory report dates a canvas sample at 1520 with a range of plus or minus 40 years, and a sample of the frame at 1535 with a range of plus or minus 30 years. The curator asks for the midpoint of the years in which both results could be true.
questions.explanation: The canvas range runs from 1480 to 1560 and the frame range from 1505 to 1570, so both are true between 1505 and 1560. The midpoint of that shared span is 1532.5.
questions.hint: Find where the two ranges overlap before taking its middle.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shared theme in two cultures
questions.learningObjective: Compare a shared theme without claiming a shared origin

stimulus.body: A planning exhibition pairs a painted wall of pilgrims crossing a river with a hand-painted scroll of a mountain shrine. The curator writes that both show travellers moving toward a holy place, and asks what that shared theme can support.

questions.stem: The board's curator proposes a joint display and asks the planning office to decide how far the shared theme of pilgrimage allows the two works to be linked.

options.text: One of the works should be presented as the model the other imitates, since one is clearly the older.
options.misconception: sees a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: The shared subject shows the two traditions borrowed the same pattern from one another in either direction.
options.misconception: treats one shared motif as one origin

options.text: The two works can be compared as separate answers to a shared theme, with no shared training implied.
The theme is too general to serve as evidence, so the two works should not be shown together at all.
options.misconception: takes a shared theme as a shared workshop

questions.explanation: Shared subjects appear across distant traditions and travel widely, so the theme shows parallel solutions rather than contact. The display can compare how each tradition handled it.
questions.hint: Ask what a shared subject can and cannot prove.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why comparison is not a ranking
questions.learningObjective: Separate a comparison of features from a ranking of artists
questions.stem: Two works are proposed for the same wall: a local painter's harbour scene and a better-known work of the same period. The board asks the curator, in two stages, to say first what can legitimately be compared and then what the label may conclude.

options.text: Choose the work with the earliest date, because an early work influences everything painted after it.
options.misconception: assumes the pattern continues forever

options.text: Decide which work is the better painting, then let the more famous artist represent the pair.
options.misconception: sees a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: Compare the market values of the two works, since value measures the quality of the handling.
options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

options.text: Compare the features the two works share, then state only that comparison and claim no superiority.

questions.explanation: Comparison sets two works against stated features so that differences and likenesses can be described. It says nothing about which painter is better, so a ranking would overstate the evidence.
questions.hint: Do the comparison first, and leave any verdict out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an accession number records
questions.stem: At the depot museum every object carries an accession number written on a tie-on label. The curator explains that a work filed as a gift of 1974 carries a number that also encodes its former collection. What does the numbering scheme do?

options.text: It certifies that the object is an original rather than a later copy of a known picture.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: It records the object's place in the museum's own sequence of acquisitions and earlier ownership.
It records the market value the object carried when it entered the museum collection.
options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

options.text: It names the artist, because any accession number can be looked up to reveal a maker.
options.misconception: assumes a label was written by a scholar

questions.explanation: Accession numbers record the order in which the museum acquired an object, sometimes with its earlier owner. They identify and trace, and do not certify authorship, value or originality.
questions.hint: Numbers identify and trace; they do not certify quality.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that resists its label
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey of features against a claimed subject
questions.stem: A survey of the station murals compares eight painted features with a published town plan of 1890. Five features, including the bridge and the market cross, match the plan exactly, while three are buildings the plan does not show at all.

options.text: The mural was painted from memory by a workman who had never seen the town, so every feature is unreliable.
options.misconception: assumes an error makes every feature worthless

options.text: The mural must be a later copy of a lost painting, because three of its buildings are in no record.
options.misconception: treats a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: The mural records the town in part and adds invention in part, so the label should say documentary.
The town plan is the later document, because published plans were corrected as towns grew and changed.
options.misconception: assumes a printed plan is always the newest source

questions.explanation: Features that match the plan show the painter used local knowledge, while the three unmatched buildings show invention. A label should describe both rather than call the mural wholly documentary.
questions.hint: Separate matching features from the ones that do not match.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Dating by style
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a dated work can date others by style
questions.stem: A curator explains that a painter's handling changed noticeably over a career, and asks the board to explain why a signed and dated work can help date an unsigned picture that resembles it.

answer.exemplar: A signed and dated work fixes the style that its painter was using at a known moment, so an unsigned picture that shares those features must be near that moment in the career. The unsigned work can then be given a range, though the range is only as firm as the comparison of features, and other painters may have copied the same manner.

questions.explanation: A dated work anchors a style in time, and an unsigned work close to it can be placed nearby. The result is a range, not a point, and a shared manner can also be copied by others.
questions.hint: A dated example anchors a style at a known moment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Science that dates the support
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a support size from stated measurements
questions.stem: A lining canvas was ordered for a painted panel that measures 58 by 44 centimetres, and the order specified that the lining should be 12 centimetres larger in each direction so that it could be turned over the edges. What length of lining was ordered along the panel's longer side?
questions.explanation: The longer side of the panel is 58 centimetres, and the lining was specified as 12 centimetres larger in that direction. Adding the two gives 70 centimetres, which is the length of lining ordered.
questions.hint: Add the extra allowance to the longer measurement.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: State what a laboratory report can and cannot date

stimulus.body: The report finds no pigment later than 1700 in the panel's upper layer, and dates a sample of the wood to 1668 plus or minus 12 years. The report notes that the picture was transferred to a new canvas in 1884 and repainted along a fold in 1902.

questions.stem: The board must say what this laboratory report is able to establish about the date of the picture on the panel.

options.text: It shows the picture is a later copy, because a genuine panel would never have been transferred at all.
options.misconception: assumes any later treatment proves a false object

options.text: It dates the whole object to 1668, since every layer of a painting must be of the same age as its wood.
options.misconception: assumes a dated support dates the image

options.text: It proves the picture was made in 1902, because that is the most recent treatment recorded.
options.misconception: takes the latest event as the making of the work

options.text: It dates the wood, rules out painting after 1700, and leaves the 1884 transfer date as a documented event.

questions.explanation: The report gives a range for the timber and a limit for the picture layer, not a date. A later transfer or repainting is an event in the object's history rather than its making.
questions.hint: Separate a limit from a date and an event from a making.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why comparison is not a ranking
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a descriptive comparison from a verdict
questions.stem: The board discusses two treatments of the same subject, one by a famous painter and one by a local artist, and the chair notes that the display has attracted complaints that the pair has been arranged to flatter the famous name.

options.text: The complaint is fair, because any pairing of two works is inevitably a judgement between them.
options.misconception: sees a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: The complaint rests on reading the display as a contest, whereas the display sets two works side by side.
The complaint is unfair, because the local artist is the better painter and the display proves it.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

options.text: The complaint should be settled by removing the local painter's work from the display altogether.
options.misconception: assumes a display must be decided by taste

questions.explanation: A side-by-side display compares two treatments of a subject so visitors see how each was handled. It becomes a ranking only if a claim of superiority is added, and the comparison adds none.
questions.hint: Ask whether any claim of superiority has been added.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Interpret gaps in a collection register
questions.stem: The depot's accession register lists forty-one objects with numbers, and thirty-four of them carry a note of the year of acquisition. Seven numbers are crossed through, and the curator explains that crossings mark objects later returned to their owners.

options.text: The register proves that the remaining seven objects never existed, because no record survives for them.
options.misconception: reads silence in a record as denial

options.text: The register shows that thirty-four objects were stolen, since a crossed number means a missing object.
options.misconception: reads a crossed entry as a loss without evidence

options.text: The register records thirty-four acquisitions, and the crossed entries show members withdrawn.
The register shows the collection was assembled in one year, since all surviving numbers carry that date.
options.misconception: assumes a shared label means a shared history

questions.explanation: A register entry records an acquisition, and a crossed entry marks a withdrawal rather than a theft. The surviving notes document thirty-four acquisitions, and the gaps show members have left.
questions.hint: A crossed entry records a change, not a disappearance.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that resists its label
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a landscape may not be topographical
questions.stem: A mural in the station concourse is described in the display list as a topographical view of the harbour, and a curator asks the board to explain why that label does not fit a painting in which the harbour buildings are rearranged to frame a distant mountain.

answer.exemplar: A topographical view records a place as it can be observed from a viewpoint, and the painter here has moved buildings out of their true positions, altered the shoreline and inserted a mountain that does not stand near the harbour. The work therefore works as an arrangement of remembered and imagined elements, and calling it topographical describes a place it does not actually show.

questions.explanation: A topographical claim means the work records a place as seen, and rearranged buildings and an invented mountain break that claim. The label should call it an arrangement, not a record.
questions.hint: Check whether the features sit where the place has them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Dating by style
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the latest year consistent with two style ranges
questions.stem: A poster's lettering matches a lettering style the archive documents as in use from 1924 to 1936, and its palette matches one the archive documents from 1928 to 1931. The curator asks for the latest year in which both features could be true at once.
questions.explanation: The lettering style runs from 1924 to 1936 and the palette style from 1928 to 1931, so they overlap only between 1928 and 1931. The latest year in which both hold is 1931.
questions.hint: Take the year at which the shorter style range ends.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Science that dates the support
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the support from the painted surface

stimulus.body: A station painting has a plain weave of a kind produced on wide looms, and the depot holds a note that the same stretch of fabric was used for a curtain acquired in 1911. The painting itself shows a tram line that opened in 1934.

questions.stem: A curator asks the board which of these three facts can be used to date the painting, and why.

options.text: None of the three facts helps, because a picture's date comes from its style and never from its subject.
options.misconception: ignores what the paint layer can show

options.text: The curtain acquisition of 1911 dates the painting, because the fabric must have been new when bought.
options.misconception: assumes a dated support dates the image

options.text: The tram line dates the painting exactly, since a painter could only record a line already open.
options.misconception: treats a date in the picture as a date of making

options.text: The tram line gives the earliest possible date, and the reused curtain suggests the support may be older.

questions.explanation: A feature in a picture sets the earliest year it can show, while a support already in use can be older than the painting. Style and documents supply the rest, and no one fact gives a date.
questions.hint: Some facts give a floor, others give a possibility.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a report can establish in two steps
questions.stem: A report on a painted screen lists the laboratory's findings, and the board must answer in two stages: first what the report positively establishes, and then what it cannot establish about the maker of the picture.

options.text: Establish the date range, then name the artist whose pigments appear most often in the sample.
options.misconception: assumes a dated support dates the image

options.text: Establish the materials and date range, then note that neither identifies the hand that painted the screen.
Establish the materials, then declare the work a copy because the pigments are common ones.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: Establish the date range, then accept the sender's attribution, since reports confirm what was sent.
options.misconception: assumes a label was written by a scholar

questions.explanation: A report describes materials and gives ranges, and those are its findings. Naming a hand is a separate argument the report does not make, so the board should keep the two apart.
questions.hint: Materials and dates are findings; a name is a claim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shared theme in two cultures
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a shared subject does and does not imply
questions.stem: A travelling display pairs a painted water jar from one region with a scroll showing a court feast, and the curator asks what the pairing on the subject of hospitality actually demonstrates.

options.text: That the objects were made for the same patron, since the theme of hospitality points to a shared household.
options.misconception: reads a shared subject as a shared owner

options.text: That one of the two traditions took the theme from the other, since the subject could not occur twice.
options.misconception: treats one shared motif as one origin

options.text: That both traditions found the theme worth treating, which invites comparison but proves no shared origin.
That the scroll is a copy of the jar, because painted vessels and painted scrolls travelled together in trade.
options.misconception: assumes a shared theme as a shared workshop

questions.explanation: Themes such as hospitality are common and travel, so two works on one subject show separate answers to a common idea. That supports comparison and nothing stronger, and no borrowing follows.
questions.hint: A shared subject shows a shared idea, not a shared hand.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why comparison is not a ranking
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a comparison can and cannot establish
questions.stem: The board's officers argue about a poster pair, and the chair asks the curator to explain in a short statement what a comparison of two works does establish and where it stops.

answer.exemplar: A comparison of two works establishes which stated features they share and which differ, and it can show that each handles a problem in its own way. It stops there: it cannot show which work is better, whose influence ran in which direction, or which artist the board should prefer, because those are judgements that the compared features do not settle.

questions.explanation: Comparison describes likeness and difference, which is useful and neutral. Turning it into a ranking adds a judgement of worth that the compared features do not support.
questions.hint: Comparison describes; ranking judges.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many objects lack an identifier
questions.stem: A depot display holds 240 objects, and 210 of them carry an accession number on a tie-on label. The collections assistant asks how many objects in the display cannot yet be traced through the museum's register.
questions.explanation: Of the 240 objects in the display, 210 are already recorded, so the untraced number is the difference between the two. Subtracting 210 from 240 gives 30 objects the register does not account for.
questions.hint: Subtract the recorded objects from the total on display.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that resists its label
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features that contradict a label

stimulus.body: The notice describes a wall painting in the booking hall as a view of the market place as it stood in the 1840s. It adds that the painting shows a fountain that a photograph of 1871 shows to have been removed eleven years earlier, and an arcade that was built in 1903.

questions.stem: A visitor complains that the booking hall painting cannot show the 1840s as the notice claims, and the board asks what follows from the two details in the notice.

options.text: Nothing follows, because notices about pictures are written for visitors and carry no evidential weight.
options.misconception: assumes a label was written by a scholar

options.text: The fountain proves the picture is an 1871 copy, since the removed feature was simply copied.
options.misconception: assumes a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: The arcade shows the picture is a modern reconstruction, since a painter could not know of it.
options.misconception: treats a mixed date as proof of a modern fake

options.text: Both details are later than the claimed date, so the picture shows the square as remembered or imagined.

questions.explanation: A fountain removed in 1860 and an arcade built in 1903 are both later than the 1840s, so the picture is not a record of that decade. A notice calling it a view of the period overstates it.
questions.hint: Compare each feature in the notice with the dates given.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Dating by style
questions.learningObjective: Date a work from two dated examples of a style
questions.stem: Two dated examples of a poster style are used to date an undated sheet, and the board asks the curator to reason in two stages: first to fix the span that the style covers, and then to place the undated sheet inside it.

options.text: Use the later of the two examples as the date, since a style continues unchanged until it is replaced.
options.misconception: assumes the pattern continues forever

options.text: Use the two dated examples to bound the style, then place the sheet within that span as the evidence allows.
Use the earlier example as the date, since the sheet is probably a copy of the first surviving example.
options.misconception: assumes a later work copies the first one

options.text: Use the average of the two dates, since the undated sheet must fall midway between the known examples.
options.misconception: believes a midpoint is always the best estimate

questions.explanation: Dated examples bound the period in which that manner was current, and an undated sheet close to it can be placed inside those bounds. The bounds do not fix a single year.
questions.hint: Two dated examples give you limits, not a midpoint.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Science that dates the support
questions.learningObjective: Explain what dating the support contributes
questions.stem: A curator explains how the support of a painting can be dated, and asks the board which contribution this makes to the study of a work that is still undated.

options.text: It supplies the name of the painter, since the tree species narrows the workshop to a single region.
options.misconception: takes the material as proof of the maker

options.text: It supplies the date of the picture, because painters normally work on panels the same year they are made.
options.misconception: assumes a dated support dates the image

options.text: It supplies the earliest possible date for the picture, since no painter can work before the panel exists.
It supplies no information at all, because a support can be replaced at any time without altering the picture.
options.misconception: ignores what the paint layer can show

questions.explanation: A dated support sets a floor: the picture cannot be earlier than the material that carries it. It leaves the date open above that floor, since panels were often held before use.
questions.hint: The support sets a floor for the picture's date.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: Interpret two dates given in one report
questions.stem: A laboratory report gives two dates for one object: a wood sample dated 1497 plus or minus 15 years, and a textile sample dated 1520 plus or minus 25 years. The report notes that the textile was cut from a fabric made in the 1530s.

options.text: The two dates should be averaged, because a single object must have one date and the average is fairest.
options.misconception: believes a midpoint is always the best estimate

options.text: The two dates disagree, so one of the two samples must have been mislabelled in the laboratory.
options.misconception: assumes two results on one object must conflict

options.text: The textile date of 1520 is the date of the picture, since textiles are fitted to paintings at the time.
options.misconception: takes the newest material as the making date

options.text: The wood and the textile are supports of different ages, so the object was assembled over time.

questions.explanation: Two supports of different ages show the object was put together over time, and the note about the fabric supports that reading. A difference between results is a fact to interpret, not an error.
questions.hint: Two supports can belong to one object of several dates.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shared theme in two cultures
questions.learningObjective: Explain a shared theme without a claim of influence
questions.stem: An exhibition pairs a painted panel of a widow at a grave with a hand-painted sheet of the same subject from another region, and the curator asks the board to write the display's introductory note without implying that either tradition borrowed from the other.

answer.exemplar: Both works show the same subject, a woman mourning at a grave, and each tradition treated the theme with its own conventions of pose, dress and setting. The pairing shows that the theme was current in two places at once, which makes it a good subject for comparison, and it says nothing about the movement of designs or painters between them.

questions.explanation: A shared subject shows two traditions found the theme worth treating, and comparing their solutions is illuminating. The subject alone gives no basis for borrowing.
questions.hint: Say what parallel solutions look like, not who copied whom.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why comparison is not a ranking
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the average size of groups in a comparison
questions.stem: A catalogue of the depot collection numbers sixty works and arranges them into six groups by period of making. The board asks how many works, on average, fall into each of the six groups.
questions.explanation: The catalogue lists sixty works in six groups, so the average group holds the total divided by the number of groups. Sixty divided by six is ten works, an average that says nothing about quality.
questions.hint: Divide the total number of works by the number of groups.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Describe the elements of a collection record

stimulus.body: The record for a painting gives its number, its title as used in the museum, the name of the maker as recorded, the date, the materials, the measurements, the condition at the last inspection, and the history of its ownership so far as it is known.

questions.stem: Which elements of the record allow a reader to trace the object, and what the record as a whole is for?

options.text: The title alone allows a reader to trace the object, since titles are unique within any museum collection.
options.misconception: assumes a label was written by a scholar

options.text: The number and the ownership history let a reader trace the object, and the record preserves what is known.
The measurements allow a reader to trace the object, since size identifies a picture securely.
options.misconception: confuses a work with its framework

options.text: The condition note allows a reader to trace the object, because it records where the picture has been kept.
options.misconception: believes a condition report dates a work

questions.explanation: A record preserves identifying, descriptive and historical information so an object can be found, checked and studied later. The number and the ownership history do the tracing.
questions.hint: A record lets a later reader find and understand the object.

options.text: Accept the note as the artist's own signature, then use it to settle the value of the canvas for insurance.
options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

options.text: Accept the note as the artist's own signature, then date the canvas by the year the painter died.
options.misconception: believes a signature proves the hand

options.text: Compare the note with the handling, then keep or set aside the name according to what the picture shows.
Set the note aside without checking, then publish the canvas as anonymous so that the error cannot spread.
options.misconception: ignores what the paint layer can show

questions.explanation: A note on the back is evidence to be checked against the picture, and it may be a later addition. Checking it first is the safe order, since a reverse name can be copied or mislaid.
questions.hint: Check the note against the object before relying on it.

questions.stem: The board has two versions of a poster announcing a new service, and the curator notes that the later one uses a heavier outline and flatter colour, and that the first appears on a platform dated 1912.

options.text: The style changed when the service changed, so the second poster must show a new, better-designed service.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

options.text: The first poster is a later copy, since a printer normally reproduces the poster already on the platform.
options.misconception: assumes a later work copies the first one

options.text: The two posters were made at the same time by different printers, since style varies from press to press.
options.misconception: assumes contractor habits erase design standards

options.text: The first poster shows the earlier style, and the change in outline and colour marks a later phase.

questions.explanation: A dated example fixes one style at one moment, so a poster carrying it comes at or after that date, and a change in handling marks a later phase. Style gives an order, not a verdict.
questions.hint: Use the dated poster to fix one style at a known moment.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a modern material can contradict a date
questions.stem: A curator explains why a modern binder in the paint of a supposedly sixteenth-century panel would undermine the attribution, and asks the board to explain the reasoning in a short statement.

answer.exemplar: A panel painted in the sixteenth century could only have been painted with materials that existed then, and a modern binder in the paint layer cannot be part of the original execution. Its presence shows that the surface has been worked on, or that the panel has been repainted, so the picture's age and the age of its support have to be argued separately.

questions.explanation: Materials that postdate the claimed making are evidence about the surface, and they show the panel was worked on later. The support may be old while the surface is not.
questions.hint: A material that did not exist yet cannot be original.

questions.learningObjective: Compare treatments of a shared theme

stimulus.body: The display places a wall painting of a harvest festival beside a painted scroll of a harvest festival. In the wall painting the figures dance in a ring around a stack of sheaves, and in the scroll they walk in a line carrying fruit toward a seated figure.

questions.stem: The board asks what the display note should say about the two harvest scenes, given that the figures are arranged differently in each.

options.text: That the scroll copies the wall painting, since the ring of dancers was the standard way to show a harvest.
options.misconception: treats one shared motif as one origin

options.text: That each tradition organised the same theme in its own way, so the pair invites comparison of arrangement.
That the wall painting is the older of the two, since a ring of dancers is an older custom than a procession.
options.misconception: sees a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: That the two works are less interesting together than separately, because they show the same subject twice.
options.misconception: assumes shared themes mean shared artists

questions.explanation: The same subject is organised differently in each work, which is what a comparison of two traditions can show. Arrangement alone establishes no borrowing and no ranking.
questions.hint: Compare how each work organises the shared subject.

options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

options.text: Visitors supplied a ranking the label did not ask for, which shows comparison is easily read as a contest.
Visitors ignored the label, so the display should be rewritten to make the comparison even plainer.
options.misconception: assumes a label was written by a scholar

questions.explanation: The survey shows a comparative display is read as a contest even when the text does not rank the artists. That is a fact about how visitors read, and it argues for careful labelling.
questions.hint: The reading may come from the display, not the label.

questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a collection is documented
questions.stem: The board's officers ask the curator to explain in a short statement why a museum records its objects at all, and what would be lost if it did not.

answer.exemplar: A record captures what is known and where it came from, so that a work can be found again, checked against new evidence and understood by people who never saw it. Without records the museum would hold objects whose dates, makers and histories could no longer be established, and every future argument about them would have to start from scratch.

questions.explanation: Documentation preserves identity, evidence and history so a collection stays usable rather than merely accumulating objects. Without it, later research has nothing to check against.
questions.hint: Records keep a collection usable after the staff have gone.

options.text: The name must be right, since frames and portraits were always made for the same person they name.
options.misconception: believes a frame label settles the sitter

options.text: The sitter dressed in the 1690s, so the picture must be a portrait of someone born after 1690.
options.misconception: reads a costume detail as a date of making

options.text: The picture shows two sitters painted in different decades, so the board should split the canvas in two.
options.misconception: assumes a mixed style proves two artists

options.text: The frame label and the evidence disagree, so the name is a tradition about the picture, not an identity.

questions.explanation: A name on a frame can be old and still be wrong, and here the costume and the handling point in different directions. The board should record the disagreement, not hide it.
questions.hint: Treat the frame label as evidence, not as a conclusion.

options.misconception: assumes the pattern continues forever

options.text: Bound the style with the dated examples, then place the sheet inside those limits without fixing a year.
Take the earlier dated example as the date, since the sheet was probably copied from the first of the two.
options.misconception: assumes a later work copies the first one

options.text: Average the two dates, since a sheet between two examples must fall exactly halfway between them.
options.misconception: believes a midpoint is always the best estimate

questions.explanation: Dated examples bound the years in which that manner was current, and a sheet that follows it belongs inside those limits. Such sheets are often printed later from an old design.
questions.hint: Use the dated examples as brackets, not as a midpoint.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the scope of laboratory findings

stimulus.body: The report identifies the wood as oak and the ground as chalk with a bound animal glue size. It dates the wood to 1712 plus or minus 9 years, finds the lead white consistent with lead made in the 1680s, and notes a resin varnish applied in 1954 that is not original.

questions.stem: The report's findings support one date more securely than the others, and the board must say which.

options.text: The 1954 date, since that is the year of the varnish the laboratory identified in the surface.
options.misconception: takes the latest event as the making of the work

options.text: The 1712 date, since the wood and the paint must always be of the same age in a finished picture.
options.misconception: assumes a dated support dates the image

options.text: The 1680s, since a lead white made then was available to the painter and matches the ground described.
No date is supported, since a report that describes a varnish cannot also describe a painting.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

questions.explanation: The lead white gives material evidence that belongs to the original execution, and the wood date of 1712 is a floor for the support. A varnish of 1954 says nothing about the painting.
questions.hint: Ask which finding belongs to the original execution.

options.text: Establish the shared subject, then conclude that the older work is the source for the later one.
options.misconception: sees a difference of date as a ranking

options.text: Establish the shared subject, then conclude that one tradition must have taken the theme from the other.
options.misconception: treats one shared motif as one origin

options.text: Establish the shared subject, then conclude that the two works were made for the same patron and shrine.

questions.topic: Why comparison is not a ranking
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a comparison should not be turned into a verdict
questions.stem: The board compares a much-copied painting with its rarer original, and the chair observes that visitors say the copy is better because it is more legible to modern eyes, and asks what the board should do with that response.

options.text: Adopt the response, since a comparison that leaves quality unsaid is incomplete and unhelpful to visitors.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

options.text: Record the response as a reading of the display, and keep the label on the shared features.
Reject the response outright, since untrained visitors cannot judge paintings and their opinions count little.
options.misconception: assumes a display must be decided by taste

options.text: Rehang the pair so the copy is shown first, since the order of hanging is the board's only guide to quality.
options.misconception: sees a difference of date as a ranking

questions.explanation: Visitors' preferences are data about how a display is read, not evidence about the works. Keeping the label on compared features avoids turning a comparison into a verdict.
questions.hint: A visitor's reaction is about the display, not the works.

questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a condition report contributes
questions.stem: The depot's collections assistant explains what a condition report adds to the record of a work, and asks the board to say why such reports are kept at intervals rather than once.

answer.exemplar: A condition report records the state of the surface at a given date, including losses, flaking, old repairs and any change since the last inspection. Keeping a series of them lets a curator see how a work is moving, since one report gives only a snapshot, and it warns anyone planning a treatment or a display what handling the object can bear.

questions.explanation: A condition report is a dated snapshot of the object's state, and a series of them shows the rate of change. One report is only a moment in the object's history.
questions.hint: One report is a moment; a series shows movement.

options.text: It can be dated to any year after 1961, since styles are never used again once replaced.
options.misconception: assumes the pattern continues forever

options.text: It can be dated to 1961 exactly, since a lettering style was used for one year only.
options.misconception: assumes a style lasts only one year

questions.explanation: A style change gives a floor, since the new manner was in use from the year it was adopted. It gives no ceiling, because the manner may continue for decades and a tile may be moved.

options.misconception: takes the material as proof of the maker

options.text: The picture must be a later copy, because an artist always paints on a support made that same year.
options.misconception: assumes a dated support dates the image

options.misconception: assumes two results on one object must conflict

Fifteen years, because that is the amount by which the upper limit moved.

questions.stem: An exhibition brings together a painted jar from one region and a carved panel from another, and the curator asks the board to state in a short note what may honestly be claimed about the common subject of feasting.

answer.exemplar: Both works show people eating and drinking together, and the subject was current in both regions at roughly the same time, which makes the pairing a useful one for comparison. What cannot be claimed is that either people or designs travelled between the two regions, since the subject travelled far more easily than objects, artists or stories did.

questions.explanation: A common subject establishes a relationship worth examining and no more. Subjects travel with stories, so the honest claim is a comparison of two treatments, not contact.
questions.hint: Say that the subject travelled, not that the objects did.

options.misconception: assumes a display must be decided by taste

options.text: Note what the pairing reveals, then label the better-known work as the model the rarer one follows.

questions.hint: Manage the reading of the display, do not abandon it.

options.misconception: assumes a display must be decided by taste

options.text: It is unnecessary, since one good work always makes a neighbour look worse in the same room.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

questions.explanation: A comparison describes how two works differ and resemble each other on the chosen features, and that is its function. Whether one is better is a separate question that turns it into a ranking.
questions.hint: Comparison describes; it does not award prizes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a collection is documented
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a collection record preserves
questions.stem: The collections assistant explains what a collection record preserves and why the depot keeps its records even for objects that no visitor will see, and asks the board to agree the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A record preserves what was known at the time, including the object number, the condition, the measurements and the ownership history, so that a later curator can check a new claim against an old record and correct it. Objects that are rarely shown still answer research questions, and without records their evidence would be lost as soon as the staff who knew them retired.

questions.explanation: Records are kept so knowledge outlives the people who hold it, and so later claims can be checked rather than accepted. A collection's value grows with its record as much as with the objects.
questions.hint: Records let a later curator check a later claim.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that resists its label
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a work may resist the label applied to it
questions.stem: Objects carry more than any label can hold, and a curator explains to the board why a work may resist the label applied to it.

answer.exemplar: A label is a short description written by someone with limited time, while the object carries features that the writer may not have noticed, may not have understood, or may have disagreed with. A work therefore resists its label whenever the evidence in the object does not match the words on the card, and the remedy is to check the card against the object rather than to adjust the object.

questions.explanation: Labels compress what is known into a few words, and objects carry more than any label can hold. Where they disagree, the label is the part that must be revised.
questions.hint: The object is the evidence; the card is the summary.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Dating by style
questions.learningObjective: Calculate years between a date and a phase's start
questions.stem: A painter's documented career runs in three phases: the first from 1881 to 1894, the second from 1895 to 1907, and the third from 1908 to 1919. An unsigned work matches the second phase and carries an inscription of 1901. How many years after the second phase began was it made?
questions.explanation: The second phase began in 1895, and the inscription dates the work to 1901. The difference between the two years is six, so the work was made six years into its phase.
questions.hint: Subtract the phase's start year from the inscribed year.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Science that dates the support
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a transfer affects what the support shows

stimulus.body: A station mural was transferred from a plastered wall to a new canvas in 1931, and the depot holds a note that the plaster was mixed with a sand found only in a quarry closed in 1898. A painted tram number on the mural corresponds to a numbering scheme used from 1904 to 1930.

questions.stem: The note and the tram number together suggest a date for the mural, and the board is asked how far to trust the pair.

options.text: The mural is a later copy, since a real wall painting would not be moved to canvas at all.
options.misconception: assumes any later treatment proves a false object

options.text: The mural was painted in 1931, since that is the year of the transfer to canvas.
options.misconception: takes the latest event as the making of the work

options.text: The wall work is likely later than 1904 and possibly before 1898, so the clues pull in opposite directions.
The mural cannot be dated, since a transfer always destroys the evidence a picture carries.
options.misconception: ignores what the paint layer can show

questions.explanation: The tram number sets a floor of 1904, and the quarry note suggests the plaster is not later than 1898, so the evidence pulls two ways. The transfer in 1931 changed the support only.
questions.hint: Some clues set a floor and others set a ceiling.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: Reason in two stages about laboratory findings
questions.stem: A report about a painted screen is sent to the board with a request for a dating decision, and the chair asks the curator to reason in two stages: first to state what the report establishes, and then to say what decision can properly be taken.

options.text: State the materials and date range, then rule the screen out, since a range cannot support a decision.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: State the materials and date range, then take the central year of the range as the date of the screen.
options.misconception: believes a midpoint is always the best estimate

options.text: State the materials and date range, then accept the earliest year in the range as the date of the screen.
options.misconception: takes the oldest record as the truest

options.text: State the materials and date range, then adopt a range for the record without turning it into a year.

questions.explanation: The first stage reports the findings, and the second asks what they can support. A range is the honest output of a report, and turning it into a single year goes beyond the evidence.
questions.hint: A range can be recorded; a single year cannot be read off.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory report can date
questions.learningObjective: Set out the limits of what a report can establish
questions.stem: A laboratory report on a station painting is summarised on the board in two stages, and the chair asks the curator to check first the findings and then the conclusions drawn from them, and to say what the report cannot settle.

options.text: Check the findings, keep the conclusions within them, and note that the picture must be a copy.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: Check the findings, keep the conclusions within them, and note that the maker and the exact year remain open.
Check the findings, keep the conclusions within them, and note that works should not be labelled by maker.
options.misconception: assumes a label was written by a scholar

options.text: Check the findings, keep the conclusions within them, and note that a date range settles any dispute.
options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

questions.explanation: A report supports the statements it makes and no others, so findings and conclusions must be checked against each other. The maker and an exact year remain open.
questions.hint: Ask which conclusions the findings actually support.
